⚡ SUNDAY METALS PULSE — SEPTEMBER 27 ⚡

Four metals. One pulse. No noise.

The week ends with a fascinating divergence:

Industrial metals are screaming SUPPLY.

Precious metals are fighting the FED.

☢️ URANIUM

Another week, another reminder that the nuclear fuel cycle is getting strategic.

Framatome just signed the first commercial contract to supply >5% enriched fuel to an operating US reactor.

X-energy’s new US TRISO fuel facility also reached another construction milestone.

Meanwhile Niger signed an agreement clearing the way toward restarting development of the Madaouela uranium project.

More reactors.
More advanced fuel.
More enrichment capacity needed.

And Kazatomprom recently warned it could easily sell ALL its uranium production into Eastern markets.

The West still needs to secure its pounds.

⚡ COPPER

This is where things are getting VERY interesting.

Copper is hovering around $15,000/t.

Shanghai warehouse stocks have collapsed roughly 70% since June.

LME available stocks are tightening.

The cash market has flipped into backwardation.

Chinese import premiums are near four-year highs.

Yes, Escondida has restarted after its disruption.

But the bigger problem remains:

Copper inventories are piling up in the US while metal becomes increasingly scarce elsewhere.

AI + grids + electrification are colliding with years of insufficient mine investment.

🥈 SILVER

Silver ends the week around $64.

But underneath the price weakness, physical supply keeps throwing up warning signs.

Endeavour Silver’s Guanaceví mine just suffered a ball-mill failure.

Processing capacity:

Normal → ~1,100 t/day
Now → ~600 t/day

Repairs are expected to take around THREE WEEKS.

Meanwhile:

COMEX registered silver remains below 100 Moz.

India is returning to the physical market.

Mine supply remains essentially stagnant.

2026 is still expected to mark the SIXTH consecutive global silver deficit.

Solar thrifting is real.

So is the deficit.

The next thing I want to see?

Investment demand accelerating while inventories keep falling.

That could change this market FAST.

🥇 GOLD

Gold ends the week around $4,275 after another tough week.

The culprit isn’t difficult to find:

US 10Y >5%.
Sticky inflation.
Hawkish Fed.
More rate hikes being priced.

Gold is now down sharply from its 2026 highs.

But here’s the paradox:

The very forces hurting gold today — enormous debt, high borrowing costs, geopolitical instability and persistent inflation — strengthen the longer-term monetary case for owning it.

The battle is simple:

5%+ yields vs monetary insurance.

For now, yields are winning.

🔥 MY SETUP FOR NEXT WEEK

☢️ Uranium — watch contracting and spot activity. The fuel-cycle buildout continues.

⚡ Copper — watch LME/Shanghai inventories. Physical tightness is becoming difficult to ignore.

🥈 Silver — watch COMEX registered stocks and Indian demand. Below 100 Moz keeps my attention.

🥇 Gold — watch US yields. A reversal from 5% could change sentiment quickly.

The common denominator?

SUPPLY.

You can print money.

You can build another data center.

You can announce another reactor.

But you cannot manufacture uranium, copper, silver or gold overnight.

That’s why I keep watching my four metals.

Every. Single. Day.

Hello, everyone,

This month, pain came for us too.

The Joker named his pain Batman. We named ours $MRNA.

We cowards saw storm clouds gathering over the markets and decided to take shelter. We concentrated the portfolio in stocks that should fall less when the market drifts down.

In our field, these are lower-risk stocks because they have already passed the pivotal stage, received approval, or successfully launched their products.

The patent cliff is here, and the big companies need sales now. So these stocks are currently among the main acquisition targets.

And then $MRNA happened to us.

Mario Bros was just a classic. first game i played on my NES. game with Duck Hunt and the zapper and i got the one with the Power Pad bundled in with World Class Track Meet

Zelda was the first open world exploration game i (and most other people) had ever played. so many secrets on the map that we used to scour strategy guides and discuss it with friends at school. tried bombing every wall in every dungeon

Mega Man 3 didn't invent the formula, but it basically perfected it. the graphics and soundtrack and bosses were just peak

Civilization 1 was probably the first serious strategy game i played on the family's 286 PC. Civ 2 would eventually be a big leap, but 1 was truly epic for the time. really felt like you were managing an empire and piqued my interest in places around the world

Sim City 1 on PC was an epic management simulator. it is probably still better than most city builder shovel ware on mobile app stores. had to really manage a budget to make it work

Streets of Rage 2 was the quintessential beat 'em up brawler. amazing graphics and soundtrack. one of the most fun games you could get together with your friends and just play. closet thing we had to Final Fight at home

Warcraft II was real-time strategy basically perfected, with an engaging story and characters and art style to boot. but what made this one shine was playing it with friends (modem to modem), and later with IPX over TCP/IP tools like Kali. absolutely crazy experience playing this thing on the internet with other people

Quake is probably the greatest FPS ever created. fully unlocked camera. felt like it came from the future. and running GL Quake with a Monster 3D or similar graphics card was a defining experience. rich online IRC and web communities. amazing mods like CTF and Team Fortress. no other shooter since has done what this one did for me

anyways, once every cycle there comes a product that is incredibly K-shaped with many losers and few winners.

it is ironic and poetic that this comes from the space with the most K-shaped outcomes, fuelled by people who want to get out of the lower income bracket into the upper income bracket, but they choose to do so by playing games that inherently favor a large amount of losers vs a small amount of winners. 

basically, it's like going to the casino in order to get rich. i used to get upset as well over this sort of thing, but over time, after seeing this play out every cycle, with first NFTs, then memecoins, then exchanges, then now fomo, i have come to appreciate the Matt Levine stance on this. It goes something like this:

https://t.co/XYdbmA8nse
"
1. Anyone can invest all they want in a diversified portfolio of approved investments (non-penny-stock public companies, mutual funds and exchange-traded funds with modest fees, insured bank accounts, etc.).

2. Anyone can also invest in any other dumb investment; you just have to go to the local office of the SEC and get a Certificate of Dumb Investment. (Anyone who sells dumb non-approved investments without requiring this certificate from buyers goes to prison.)

3. To get that certificate, you sign a form. The form is one page with a lot of white space. It says in very large letters: “I want to buy a dumb investment. I understand that the person selling it will almost certainly steal all my money, and that I would almost certainly be better off just buying index funds, but I want to do this dumb thing anyway. I agree that I will never, under any circumstances, complain to anyone when this investment inevitably goes wrong. I understand that violating this agreement is a felony.”

4. Then you take the form to an SEC employee, who slaps you hard across the face and says “really???” And if you reply “yes really” then she gives you the certificate.

5. Then you bring the certificate to the seller and you can buy whatever dumb thing he is selling.

6. If an article ever appears in the Wall Street Journal in which you (or your lawyer) are quoted saying that you were just a simple dentist, didn’t understand what you were buying and were swindled by the seller’s flashy sales pitch, then you go to prison.

I am open to compromise on the details. The point is that the right general approach to the problem of people buying dumb investments is to give them much, much, much clearer and starker and scarier warnings before they invest, and then much, much, much less sympathy if they do it anyway.
"

and even so, last cycle, it was more justfiable to blame pumpfun. this cycle, people blame the platform used to ape pumpfun and similar coins. what's up with that? have you guys seen the stats on Binance? it will be way worse than whatever you see on here. 

that's like - instead of blaming the casino, you blame the car that you took to drive here. and you blame the car manufacturer for manufacturing the car

no one is forcing you to buy these things. no one is forcing you to buy obvious scams, obvious projects that have no due diligence. yet you do it anyway

quite frankly, this is the epitome of people who make stupid decisions and then blame other people for making stupid decisions available to them. "oh why did you make me make a stupid decision" 

i have always believed in financial literacy yes. i believe in educating people and teaching people how to fish. it is the basis of my paid subscription. i do believe that the system doesn't do enough to teach you about finance, the world of inflation, etc. 

however too many people seem to be very very risk-on when it comes to managing their own money. i have never understood this tbh. people will scoff at paying $25 for a drink at a cafe, but throw $250 into a random investment? count me in!

no one would think that with 0 experience they could do a better job than a dentist, or with 0 experience they could play the piano better than a professional. but with 0 experience, you can somehow beat the market and invest in the thing that goes up 100x. 

perhaps the better analogy is poker. for some reason people sit down and then magically think they are suddenly a god at poker with no experience, when they're playing against poker pros. no fucking reason at all. 

anyways, i draw the line there - i think obviously at some level it is forgiveable if you truly get scammed buying something you don't understand. i did that when i first started. i spent 0.5eth, which at that time, was 4 months of my salary in the military service - on a fucking text NFT. it obviously went to 0. i was obviously upset. but i chose to understand what i did wrong. 

and so - fool me once, shame on you. fool me twice, shame on me. fool me three times, i'm a fucking retard. when you take no effort whatsoever in learning how to discern a good thing from a bad thing, that's when i think you have a gambling addiction instead of actually trying to trade. 

the thing is - the obvious counter argument is that "these things make it so accessible for people to fall prey to predators" - yes; but so do the ads on pornsites that tell you there are 50 women near you that want to date you. do you click on them? 

it's like - people have to understand that the markets aren't some free money phenomenon. maybe that's the problem. people have this perception that the markets will make them money. it would do people much better to approach the markets with caution, the same way they approach sketchy websites on the internet. people do not come to this website for charitable purposes. would you go to the casino expecting to make money?
